title: Install & Configure
subtitle: Set up Git on your machine for the first time
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Before you can use Git, it needs to know who you are — your name and email are embedded in every commit you make. A one-time setup prevents anonymous or mis-attributed commits.
whyItExists.solution: Install Git for your OS, then run two global config commands to set your identity. This is done once and applies to all your repos.
whyItExists.whenToUse: On any new machine before using Git for the first time.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: If you're using a shared machine or CI environment, prefer per-repo config or environment variables over global config.

explainModes.beginner: Installing Git is like installing any program. After that, you tell Git your name and email with two commands. Done — you're set up for life on this machine.
explainModes.simple: Install Git (git-scm.com or your package manager). Then: git config --global user.name 'Your Name' and git config --global user.email 'you@example.com'. Check with git config --list.
explainModes.standard: --global stores config in ~/.gitconfig (your home directory). It applies to all repos. --local stores in the repo's .git/config and overrides global. --system applies to all users on the machine. The most useful settings: user.name, user.email, core.editor, init.defaultBranch.
explainModes.technical: Git config is a cascading system: system → global → local → worktree. Later levels override earlier ones. git config --list --show-origin shows all settings and which file each comes from. Conditional includes ([includeIf 'gitdir:~/work/']) let you use different identities for different directories — useful for personal vs work repos on the same machine.
explainModes.deepDive: The gitconfig format is INI-style. Values are parsed as string, bool, int, path, or color depending on the key. git config --type=bool core.bare returns 'true'/'false'. Credential helpers (credential.helper) store HTTPS credentials — macOS uses Keychain, Windows uses the Windows Credential Manager, Linux uses gnome-libsecret or a plaintext store. SSH keys (ed25519 recommended over RSA) are the more secure alternative to HTTPS passwords for authentication.

content.code:
# macOS (via Homebrew)
brew install git

# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt update && sudo apt install git

# Windows
# Download from https://git-scm.com/download/win
# Or via winget:
winget install --id Git.Git

# Verify installation
git --version
# → git version 2.45.0

content.text: These two commands are the only required setup. Run them once on each machine you use Git on.

content.code:
# Set your identity — embedded in every commit
git config --global user.name "Prashant Kumar"
git config --global user.email "prashant@example.com"

# Set default branch name to 'main' (modern standard)
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

# Set your preferred editor for commit messages
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"   # VS Code
# git config --global core.editor "nano"          # Nano (simpler)
# git config --global core.editor "vim"           # Vim

# Verify all settings
git config --list

# Colorised output (usually on by default)
git config --global color.ui auto

# Better diff output
git config --global diff.algorithm histogram

# Rebase instead of merge when pulling (cleaner history)
git config --global pull.rebase true

# Show shortcuts — list all aliases
git config --global alias.st status
git config --global alias.co checkout
git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --all"

# Where global config is stored
cat ~/.gitconfig

content.text: Use git config --list --show-origin to see every setting and which file it came from. Helpful for debugging unexpected behaviour.

questions.question: What does the --global flag do in git config --global?
options: Applies the setting to all users on the system
Applies the setting to the current repo only
Applies the setting to all repos for your user account
questions.explanation: --global saves the setting to ~/.gitconfig (your home directory) and applies to all repos you use under your account. --local applies only to the current repo. --system applies to all users on the machine.

faq.q: Can I use different emails for work and personal projects?
faq.a: Yes. Set your global config to your personal email. In each work repo, run git config --local user.email 'you@company.com' to override it for that repo only. Git's [includeIf] in .gitconfig can automate this by directory.

VS Code (code --wait) is the most user-friendly. Nano is simple and terminal-based. Vim is powerful but has a steep learning curve. If you skip this setting, Git uses the system default (often vi on macOS/Linux).

usedIn: every machine a developer works on
examples: GitHub Actions sets GIT_AUTHOR_NAME and GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL env vars for automated commits
Companies use per-directory includeIf to enforce work email on work repos
